mainEntity.name: How long do acrylic dentures typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Acrylic dentures do not have a fixed lifespan, as durability depends on many factors including how well they are cared for, how frequently they are worn, and how much the underlying bone and gum tissues change over time. On average, patients may find their dentures require relining, rebasing, or replacement after five to seven years. However, some patients may require adjustments sooner, whilst others may have satisfactory fits for longer. Regular dental reviews are important in monitoring the ongoing suitability of your denture, and your dentist will advise when changes are needed.

mainEntity.name: Will wearing dentures affect how I speak or eat?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common to notice some adjustment period when first wearing new dentures. Speech may feel slightly different initially, particularly with sounds such as "s" and "f," though most patients adapt within a few weeks with practice. Eating may also take some getting used to — starting with softer foods and gradually reintroducing a more varied diet is often recommended. Persistent difficulty speaking or eating after the initial adjustment period should be discussed with your dentist, as minor adjustments to the denture fit can often make a significant difference to comfort and function.

mainEntity.name: Can I sleep with my acrylic dentures in?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental professionals generally advise that dentures are removed during sleep. Leaving dentures in overnight does not allow the gum and bone tissues to rest and recover from the pressure of denture wear during the day. It has also been associated with a higher likelihood of developing fungal infections such as denture-related stomatitis. Removing dentures at night and cleaning and soaking them thoroughly supports both the long-term condition of the prosthesis and the health of the oral tissues. If you have specific concerns about overnight denture wear, speak with your dentist for personalised guidance.

mainEntity.name: Are partial acrylic dentures better than cobalt-chrome partial dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Each type of partial denture has distinct characteristics, and neither is universally superior — suitability depends on an individual patient's clinical situation, preferences, and budget. Acrylic partial dentures are generally more economical and easier to modify or extend, making them a practical choice for patients whose dental situation may change. Cobalt-chrome (metal-framed) partial dentures tend to be thinner, lighter, and more precisely fitting, which many patients find more comfortable over time. Your dentist will be able to discuss the relative merits of each option in the context of your specific oral health needs.

mainEntity.name: Do I still need dental check-ups if I wear full dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Regular dental check-ups remain important even for patients who wear full dentures and have no remaining natural teeth. These appointments allow your dentist to examine the health of the gum and bone tissues, assess the ongoing fit and condition of your denture, and carry out an oral cancer screening — an important routine health check for all adult patients. The frequency of review appointments will vary depending on your individual circumstances, and your dental team will advise on how often you should attend.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my denture breaks or feels loose?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your denture breaks — even if you think it is a minor crack — do not attempt to repair it yourself using household glues, as this can cause further damage and may affect the fit in a way that harms the underlying gum tissue. Contact your dental practice as soon as possible to arrange an assessment. Similarly, if your denture has become noticeably loose, this should be reviewed promptly. Loose dentures can cause sore spots, affect your ability to eat and speak, and may indicate significant changes in the underlying bone ridge that need to be assessed clinically.
